target.title: fix(feishu): pace outbound sends per target
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #14206.

Feishu outbound sends currently retry after the API returns rate-limit responses, but configured high-volume conversations can still burst several `im.message.create` / `im.message.reply` calls to the same Feishu target at once. That makes the first user-visible symptom a Feishu rate-limit error instead of a paced send queue.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an opt-in `channels.feishu.sendRateLimit.minIntervalMs` setting, with the same setting available under `channels.feishu.accounts.<id>.sendRateLimit.minIntervalMs` for per-account overrides. When configured, Feishu text, card, image, and file message sends are paced by account + receive id type + receive id. Different Feishu targets still send independently, and the default interval remains `0` so existing installs keep their current behavior unless they opt in.

## User Impact

Operators can set a small per-target send interval to avoid Feishu per-chat send bursts while keeping cross-chat throughput. Existing retry handling for Feishu 230020 / 11232 / 429 responses remains in place for server-side limits that still occur.

## Real Behavior Proof

Exact head after merging current `main`: `9378385f0745f93b109df44c541d999a5f018daf`.

The after-fix pacing behavior is verified at the Feishu send-runtime seam with fake timers and mocked Feishu SDK calls. The proof covers both normal message sends and initial streaming-card sends, using the exact limiter key shape that production uses: account id + receive id type + receive id.

Same-target configured pacing proof:

```text
config: sendRateLimit.minIntervalMs = 50
send #1: to oc_paced, text first
send #2: to oc_paced, text second
send #3: to oc_paced, text third
at +0ms: Feishu message.create called 1 time
at +49ms: Feishu message.create still called 1 time
at +50ms: Feishu message.create called 2 times
after final interval: Feishu message.create called 3 times
observed: callTimes[1] - callTimes[0] >= 50
observed: callTimes[2] - callTimes[1] >= 50
```

Distinct-target independence proof:

```text
config: sendRateLimit.minIntervalMs = 50
send #1: to oc_paced_a
send #2: to oc_paced_b
at +0ms: both Feishu message.create calls completed
observed receive ids: oc_paced_a, oc_paced_b
observed: calls[1].at - calls[0].at == 0
```

Streaming-card initial send proof:

```text
config: sendRateLimit.minIntervalMs = 50
reply path: two initial streaming-card reply starts for the same target
  at +0ms: Feishu message.reply called 1 time
  at +49ms: Feishu message.reply still called 1 time
  at +50ms: Feishu message.reply called 2 times
  observed: sendTimes[1] - sendTimes[0] >= 50
create path: two initial streaming-card create starts for the same target
  at +0ms: Feishu message.create called 1 time
  at +49ms: Feishu message.create still called 1 time
  at +50ms: Feishu message.create called 2 times
  observed: sendTimes[1] - sendTimes[0] >= 50
```

- Full CI passed on this PR head: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28164195535

Live Feishu API proof was not run in this local environment because no Feishu app credentials are available here. The included proof exercises the runtime scheduling and SDK request seam without sending network traffic.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/feishu/src/send.concurrent.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/config-schema.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/send.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/send-target.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/send.retry.test.ts`

target.title: feat: add disableBoundaryAwareCache compat option for prefix-matching prompt cache providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where DeepSeek OpenAI-compatible users lose provider prompt-cache hits after the 6.x boundary-aware cache split placed per-turn dynamic context ahead of the stable system prompt, so the large stable instruction block stopped caching and billed input tokens climbed.

Closes #94518

Related: #91018, #90583

## Why This Change Was Made

DeepSeek uses implicit prefix-matching cache, so its leading `system` message must stay byte-stable across turns for the stable instruction block to keep hitting cache. This PR adds `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache`, auto-enables it for DeepSeek, keeps only the stable prefix in the `system` message, and emits the below-boundary runtime suffix as a trailing `system`-role carrier after the conversation history. That keeps the latest user message byte-identical (so it stays a reusable prefix once it becomes history) and keeps runtime/approval/identity guidance at system/developer authority instead of demoting it into user content.

Non-goal / honest limit: when the below-boundary context genuinely changes every turn, accumulated conversation history still cannot be cached — DeepSeek persists a cache prefix unit at the end of each request, so a trailing carrier that changes each turn ends every request on different bytes. No message re-ordering can cache history under that condition; this PR restores the stable-prefix cache, not moving full-history reuse.

Xiaomi is kept opt-in — users can set `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache: true` manually, but the automatic default is DeepSeek-only until Xiaomi-specific upstream cache-contract and live-behavior evidence exists. Operators can opt back into boundary-aware behavior with `compat: { disableBoundaryAwareCache: false }`.

## User Impact

DeepSeek users keep the large stable system prompt cacheable from the first turn instead of losing it whenever below-boundary runtime context updates, which lowers billed input tokens on the cost regression #94518 reports. Behavior is unchanged for providers with native cache-control (Anthropic-style) and for sessions whose below-boundary content is already stable. Xiaomi and other providers are unaffected by default.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests (rebased on latest `origin/main`):

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.test.ts`: 44 passed, incl. system-only trailing-carrier and instruction-authority assertions
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts`: 336 passed, incl. DeepSeek trailing-carrier and byte-stable-history assertions

Types: `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json` and `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json` clean for the touched files (unrelated `ui/**` `@codemirror` module-resolution noise only). Format: `oxfmt --check` clean.

### Live DeepSeek cache proof (baseline == current main vs PR)

Each turn's request is built by the **production** `buildOpenAICompletionsParams` and sent to the real DeepSeek API (`deepseek-v4-flash`); native `usage.prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` are recorded across a growing 5-turn conversation. Scenario reproduces #94518: a large stable workspace prefix (`STABLE`, ~512 tokens) is constant, while the below-boundary runtime context changes each turn. **Baseline** keeps the suffix inside the leading `system` message (byte-identical to `origin/main`); **PR** keeps `system = STABLE` only and trails the suffix as a `system`-role carrier.

```text
                     BASELINE (== current main)     PR (this change)
turn 1 (cold):       hit=0     miss=936             hit=512   miss=424
turn 2:              hit=0     miss=1726            hit=512   miss=1214
turn 3:              hit=512   miss=2004            hit=512   miss=2004
turn 4:              hit=512   miss=2794            hit=512   miss=2794
turn 5:              hit=512   miss=3584            hit=512   miss=3584
```

Reading: on `main` the mutating `system` suffix breaks the prefix match from the first token, so the stable instruction block does **not** cache on cold turns (`hit=0` on turns 1–2; DeepSeek's automatic common-prefix detection only recovers `hit=512` from turn 3). With the PR the stable prefix is byte-stable and caches from turn 1 (`hit=512`), removing the cold-start miss on the ~512-token instruction block. Reproduced across two runs with fresh cold-start nonces; API key redacted. Payload dumps confirm the PR leaves the latest user message byte-identical and carries the suffix in a `system`-role message. Full data and the byte-stable-history / session-stable-parity cases are in the linked proof notes.

target.title: feat: advertise realtime voice provider voices in talk.catalog
target.body:
Closes #106020

AI assisted with Claude Opus 4.8 and Fable 5

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where Talk clients could not learn which voices the active realtime voice provider supports. `talk.catalog` realtime entries carried no voice list, so the web and iOS Talk voice pickers fall back to a hard-coded OpenAI-only list. With any other active realtime provider (e.g. Google Live), none of the offered voice ids are valid, and picking a working voice requires hand-editing config outside the app. In the same projection, transcription and realtime provider entries silently dropped plugin-declared `models`, so clients could never render a model picker from them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Mirrors the existing speech-provider seam: `RealtimeVoiceProviderPlugin` gains an optional `voices?: readonly string[]` that core projects into `talk.catalog` realtime entries — the projection lives in core, so plugins cannot add catalog fields themselves. Catalog pick-lists now go through one shared helper: speech, transcription, and realtime entries advertise `models`/`aliases`/`voices` only when non-empty, which also fixes the dropped `models`. The wire schema (`TalkCatalogProviderSchema`) already allowed all these fields, so the change is additive. The OpenAI plugin advertises its canonical voice list (the same set its config validation accepts); the Google plugin advertises the shared 30-name Google TTS voice inventory it already maintains — Google's Live API docs state native-audio models accept every TTS voice, and the realtime runtime forwards the configured voice id unvalidated. The SDK type and docs now pin the field's semantics: a provider-wide set of ids every supported model accepts, omitted when no such set exists. Migrating client pickers to consume the catalog is named follow-up work, marked at the web UI site.

## User Impact

Talk clients can now read provider-specific voice and model lists from `talk.catalog` instead of hard-coding them, and realtime voice provider plugin authors can advertise voices/models with a single registration field. Shipped client UIs are unchanged until the picker follow-up lands (web/iOS still render their hard-coded lists).

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/talk.test.ts extensions/openai/realtime-voice-provider.test.ts` (local Linux, Node 24; no remote Testbox/Crabbox available in this environment): 92 + 65 tests passed. Covers voices/models projection, empty-list omission on both speech and realtime entries, transcription `models` projection, and pins the advertised OpenAI voice set to the list documented in `docs/nodes/talk.md`.
- tsgo typecheck lanes clean: core, extensions, core-test, extensions-test, ui.
- oxfmt/oxlint clean on changed files.
- `plugin-sdk:api:check` OK on the rebased head — the new optional SDK field does not shift the API baseline (type aliases are recorded by name), verified by regenerating before and after.

Real setup on this PR head: fresh `pnpm build`, isolated `$OPENCLAW_HOME`, config with `talk.realtime.provider: "openai"` (no credentials configured — the catalog projection is registration-driven), gateway started with `openclaw gateway --bind loopback --allow-unconfigured`, then a real WS RPC via `openclaw gateway call talk.catalog --json`. Response contains no secrets.

target.title: fix(discord): bound stalled probe response reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord probe checks could hang after the `getMe` request returned response headers but the JSON response body stopped producing data.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord probe now reads the successful `getMe` JSON body through the bounded response reader with the existing 16 MiB cap and a per-chunk timeout tied to the probe timeout. Application metadata reads are also bounded, and the status entry point carries only the remaining caller timeout through cold lazy loading. Existing non-OK handling, malformed JSON wording, and the already-resolved bot result are preserved.

## User Impact

Discord configuration checks now return from stalled response bodies instead of waiting indefinitely. If optional application metadata stalls, the successful bot identity remains available.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/probe.intents.test.ts extensions/discord/src/channel.test.ts extensions/discord/src/api.test.ts` (`3` files, `63` tests passed)
- `git diff --check b0ebb81e89f5217397d409c996e2bbf914623a94..HEAD`
- Claude autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings

## Proof

### Exact-current-head controlled local HTTP production-path proof

Exact head: `3a470fcd81a815982a1669c4568518bb75551331`.

Command:

```text
git rev-parse HEAD
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u ALL_PROXY -u http_proxy -u https_proxy -u all_proxy timeout 30s ./node_modules/.bin/tsx --no-cache scratchpad/discord-probe-current-head-proof.ts
```

The temporary harness called the production `discordPlugin.status.probeAccount()` and `probeDiscord()` paths. It used a real loopback `node:http` server and real Node `fetch`; the existing fetch seam only rewrote the fixed Discord origin to loopback while forwarding the production request options and abort signal. No mocked `Response`, Discord traffic, or credentials were used.

Redacted transcript:

```text
3a470fcd81a815982a1669c4568518bb75551331
proof=controlled-local-http production-path=discord-status+probe
cold-status-app-stall ok=true bot=proof-bot application=undefined elapsed=290ms callerBudget=300ms socketAborted=true
normal ok=true bot=proof-bot application=app-proof elapsed=7ms
get-me-stall ok=false error="discord.probe.getMe: JSON response stalled after 140ms" elapsed=188ms socketAborted=true
recovery-after-get-me-stall ok=true bot=proof-bot application=app-proof elapsed=6ms
application-stall ok=true bot=proof-bot application=undefined elapsed=200ms callerBudget=220ms socketAborted=true
final-recovery ok=true bot=proof-bot application=app-proof elapsed=6ms
requests=11 assertions=passed
```

Observed:

- The first status probe in the process cold-loaded the lazy probe runtime. A partial application-metadata body then stalled, was aborted, and returned in `290ms` within the `300ms` caller budget; the resolved bot identity remained present and optional application metadata was omitted.
- A partial `getMe` JSON body that stopped producing bytes returned the production idle-timeout error and closed the server response before `writableEnded` (`socketAborted=true`).
- A direct stalled application-metadata response also closed before `writableEnded`, returned inside the `220ms` caller budget, and preserved `ok=true` plus the bot identity.
- Normal probes before and after the failures returned both bot and application data, demonstrating later-call recovery. All harness assertions passed with exit `0`.

Known limits: this is controlled local real-HTTP production-path proof, not live Discord. It does not claim live Discord behavior or credentialed testing. The `getMe` body protection is an idle/per-chunk timeout, not a total response deadline, so this proof covers a body that stops producing data and does not claim protection from an indefinitely slow trickle. The temporary uncommitted harness was removed after the run.


This exact-head section supersedes the earlier `f6de53aba381701e59a0554a8ffe80c9c5b76457` transcript.

target.title: fix(line): honor channelData.line.mediaKind on the reply-token path
target.body: Closes #106512 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where a LINE bot that replies to an inbound message with a video or audio attachment — and sets `channelData.line.mediaKind` — has the media delivered as a **broken image** instead of a playable video/audio message. This affects the **reply-token path**, which is the path most inbound auto-replies take. `docs/channels/line.md` states the media kind is taken from `channelData.line.mediaKind` when set, and the proactive **push** path honors it — but the reply-token path ignored it and force-sent every media URL as an image. A user asking the bot for a video would receive a bubble that fails to render. ## Why This Change Was Made The reply-token delivery in `auto-reply-delivery.ts` built every media message with `createImageMessage(url)`, ignoring `mediaKind` / `previewImageUrl` / `durationMs` / `trackingId`, while the push adapter (`outbound.ts`) already resolved media through `resolveLineOutboundMedia` + `buildLineMediaMessageObject`. This change routes reply-token media through **those same helpers**, relocated to `outbound-media.ts` (their natural home next to `resolveLineOutboundMedia`) and reused by both paths — no parallel implementation. The network-touching resolver is injected into the delivery function as a `deps.buildMediaMessage` field and wired in `monitor.ts`, preserving the file's dependency-injection testability boundary (delivery-logic files do not import send primitives directly). Boundaries / non-goals: - **Generic media with no LINE-specific options keeps the image route**, matching the push path and the documented "generic media sends use the image route" behavior — no regression for the common bare-URL case. - A media that **cannot be built** (e.g. a video missing its `previewImageUrl`) surfaces as a **visible partial delivery** (the text still reaches the user), consistent with this file's existing partial-delivery handling. - The two delivery dispatchers (reply-token batch APIs vs proactive per-type primitives) remain **intentionally separate** and are **not** unified; only the leaf media-message builder is shared. ## User Impact LINE bots that reply with `channelData.line.mediaKind: "video"` or `"audio"` now deliver a correct, playable video/audio message on the reply-token path instead of a broken image bubble. No change for text-only replies or for generic media sends without LINE-specific options. ## Evidence **Real inbound → reply-token path (redacted live transcript).** A real LINE message was sent to the test-channel bot; its **fresh reply token** drove the **actual** `deliverLineAutoReply` on this branch (real `send.ts` `replyMessageLine`, no mocks). A media-only reply is used so the video rides the reply token (a text chunk would consume it), exercising the exact changed reply-token wiring end-to-end. LINE accepted the reply: ```text [2026-07-13T17:56:43.917Z] harness listening on :3000 (ngrok -> /line) [2026-07-13T17:56:51.093Z] inbound message from U4aef1…2a replyToken=9f1eb3…22 [2026-07-13T17:56:51.094Z] agent reply payload: media-only, channelData.line.mediaKind="video" [2026-07-13T17:56:51.190Z] -> replyMessageLine (REPLY TOKEN 9f1eb3…22) types=["video"] [2026-07-13T17:56:51.505Z] deliverLineAutoReply result = {"status":"delivered","replyTokenUsed":true} ``` The `replyMessageLine (REPLY TOKEN …) types=["video"]` line is the point: driven by a real inbound message, the fixed reply-token path delivered a **video** via the reply token (`replyTokenUsed: true`) — not a downgraded image and not a push fallback. On current-main this same flow would have sent `type:"image"`. **Live LINE app — before/after (real test channel).** The exact message objects the reply path builds were delivered to a LINE chat (push and reply render identically in the client). Same source clip `https://download.samplelib.com/mp4/sample-5s.mp4` in both cases; LINE returned `HTTP 200` for both. **修復前 (Before):** the reply path forced `{"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../sample-5s.mp4"}`. LINE cannot render an mp4 as an image, so the bubble is a **broken placeholder**: **修復後 (After):** the reply path honors `mediaKind="video"` and builds `{"type":"video","originalContentUrl":".../sample-5s.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clouds.jpg"}` → a **playable video bubble**: **Deterministic repro against the real functions** (real `resolveLineOutboundMedia` + `buildLineMediaMessageObject`, the exact `monitor.ts` wiring), same input clip, three outcomes: ``` OLD reply path (hardcoded): always -> {"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clip.mp4"} NEW — channelData.line = { mediaKind:"video", previewImageUrl } -> status: delivered reply message sent: {"type":"video","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../preview.jpg"} NEW — generic media, no LINE options (parity) -> status: delivered reply message sent: {"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clip.mp4"} ``` **Unit tests** — `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-line.config.ts` on the touched suites (adds 3 reply-path media cases + a full `buildLineMediaMessageObject` / `hasLineSpecificMediaOptions` / `isLineUserTarget` suite): ``` Test Files 3 passed (3) Tests 44 passed (44) ``` **Red/green** — reverting only the reply-path media routing makes exactly the two new fix cases fail while the generic-image parity case stays green: ``` Tests 2 failed | 10 passed (12) × honors channelData.line.mediaKind ... expected "partial"/"video", received "delivered"/"image" ✓ keeps the image route for generic media without LINE-specific options ``` **Static checks** — `tsgo` extensions typecheck: pass · `pnpm lint:extensions` (oxlint): pass · `oxfmt --check` on touched files: pass. Branch **rebased onto current `main`** and re-verified. ---

target.title: feat(apps): add native mobile Automations parity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The web Control UI can manage scheduled gateway work, while the native mobile apps exposed only a partial cron surface. iOS lacked safe detail/edit/history/run/delete controls, and both mobile platforms lacked practical search and status filtering.

Closes #106145.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Use the existing `cron.*` gateway contract; no new protocol or config surface.
- Add mobile-appropriate management parity while keeping creation, cloning, and dense delivery/failure-routing editing in the Control UI.
- Preserve optimistic-concurrency safety with `expectedConfigRevision` and fail closed when the connected gateway changes.
- Track queued runs by exact `runId`, paginate the complete automation list, and preserve unsaved drafts.
- Add caller-scoped cron pagination revisions so native clients retry instead of combining pages across concurrent scheduler mutations.
- Fold in the outstanding native Skills review fixes from #105814.

## User Impact

- iOS and Android now call the feature **Automations**.
- Both apps support search plus All / Active / Paused filters.
- iOS adds configuration detail, recent history, revision-safe editing, enable/pause, Run Now tracking, and confirmed deletion.
- Android retains its existing management surface with the same product naming and discovery controls.
- Create/clone and advanced delivery/failure routing remain available in the web Control UI.

## Evidence

- Android focused unit tests: Cron management/runtime, Settings filters, and Skills management.
- iOS focused tests: 13 Automations model/revision/pagination/outcome/admission tests passed on iPhone 17 Pro / iOS 26.5.
- OpenClawKit focused tests: 9 Skills management tests passed.
- Native screenshot XCUITests: Automations and Skills screens passed on iPhone 17 Pro / iOS 26.5.
- Android source-blind behavior pass: navigation, search empty state, Active/Paused filtering, detail configuration, and management actions.
- Native localization: 4,482 source entries synchronized across all 21 locale artifacts.
- Current-main dead-export regression: `ChatSendManagedMediaFields` made module-private; focused `deadcode:exports` passed on Testbox with no runtime change.
- Screenshots posted below.

target.title: fix(media): keep host-staged images available to native vision
target.body:
Closes #106408

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users sending an image through a host-mode channel could receive a text-only native-vision turn after OpenClaw staged the attachment into the agent workspace.

## Why This Change Was Made

Host-mode staging now exposes only the unique per-turn staging directory to the preparation context, allowing the existing scoped media loader to read the rewritten path. The runner context remains unchanged so the already-prepared image is not hydrated twice. No general workspace or channel-config allowlist is widened.

## User Impact

Native-vision models receive exactly one copy of the original image bytes after managed inbound media is staged into a host agent workspace.

## Evidence

- Current `main` deterministic red: host staging succeeded, but the staged directory was absent from the preparation context and native resolution returned zero images.
- Patched green: 13/13 focused regressions and 121/121 focused plus adjacent media tests.
- The staging regression pins `MediaWorkspaceDir` to the unique staging directory rather than the agent workspace.
- The boundary regression proves that staging-root access does not expose a sibling workspace image.
- The two-pass regression proves preparation followed by runner hydration remains exactly one image.
- `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` pass on the changed surface after rebasing onto current `main`.
- Redacted live observation:

```text

provider_request.imagesCount=0
resolver_without_staging_root=0
resolver_with_staging_root=1
```

- Automated review first identified a duplicate-hydration path, then identified whole-workspace allowlist widening. The final patch carries only the unique staging directory and has regressions for both findings.

target.title: fix(msteams): sanitize internal tool-trace lines from outbound text (#90684)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

MS Teams sends assistant text to users **without** running `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText()`, so internal tool-trace lines leak into user-visible messages. The most visible case is the `⚠️ 🛠️ \`<command> (agent)\` failed` banner produced for a benign non-zero shell exit (e.g. a `grep` that finds no match → exit 1). The turn completes successfully, but the user receives an alarming "failed" message from the bot.

`msteamsChannelOutbound` had no `sanitizeText` hook at all. This is the MS Teams instance of #90684. Discord, Google Chat (#95084, merged) and WhatsApp already run the canonical sanitizer on outbound; MS Teams was missing it.

Closes part of #90684. Related: #88332, #95084 (the merged Google Chat counterpart, identical fix shape).

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `sanitizeText: ({ text }) => sanitizeAssistantVisibleText(text)` to `msteamsChannelOutbound`, reusing the canonical delivery sanitizer the other channels already use (rather than new regexes). The hook runs in the shared outbound deliver path, so it covers every text send — replies, sub-agent announces, and cron deliveries. `msteamsChannelOutbound` is now exported so the hook can be unit-tested (mirrors `googlechatOutboundAdapter`).

Out of scope: the Codex-native warning taxonomy (#88332) and threading/attachments. This is one focused MS Teams instance of the cross-channel umbrella.

## User Impact

Internal trace/failure banners (e.g. `⚠️ 🛠️ … (agent) failed` from a benign `grep` no-match) are no longer shown to MS Teams users. Legitimate assistant prose is unaffected. No config, auth, secrets, network, or tool-execution behavior changes.

## Evidence

The fix wires the canonical `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText()` into the MS Teams outbound `sanitizeText` hook. Below is copied live output / console output (stdout) from running that exact function via `node` on a live OpenClaw `2026.6.8` deployment, with the leaked banner as input:

```
IN : "Listo, ya lo cargué.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `grep -E (PV-123) /tmp/out.txt (agent)` failed"
OUT: "Listo, ya lo cargué."
```

The banner line is removed; the real assistant prose is preserved.

A new unit test exercises the actual patched adapter hook:
`pnpm vitest run extensions/msteams/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts -t "sanitizeText"` → **2 passed** (`msteams outbound sanitizeText`): asserts `msteamsChannelOutbound.sanitizeText` strips the `(agent) failed` banner and leaves ordinary prose untouched.

**Proof limitations:** the MS Teams deployment available to me runs `2026.5.28`, which predates the banner machinery (it does not generate the `(agent) failed` banner — `(agent)`/`🛠️` are absent from its payload builder), so it cannot reproduce the end-to-end leak. The after-fix evidence therefore exercises the exact canonical sanitizer this PR wires into MS Teams, captured on a live `2026.6.8` deployment, plus the adapter-hook unit test. No MS Teams client screenshot; private space/account/user details omitted.

## Risk

Highest-risk area is over-stripping legitimate content. Mitigated by reusing the canonical `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText()` (already shipping for Discord/Google Chat/WhatsApp) rather than new logic, plus the new unit test asserting ordinary prose is preserved.

AI-assisted change.



---

## Real behavior proof

Local run against this branch, pnpm 11.2.2 (frozen lockfile), vitest.

### Validation (re-runnable)

```
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/msteams/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts -t "sanitizeText"
#  Test Files 1 passed (1)   Tests 2 passed | 2 skipped (4)
# full file: Tests 4 passed (4)
```

### Before/after (patched MS Teams outbound path)

Input (identical both runs):
```
Here is your summary.
⚠️ 🛠️ `grep -E 'PV-123' /tmp/out.txt (agent)` failed
The report is ready.
```
A repro drives the real `deliver.ts` sanitize gate; BEFORE = adapter `sanitizeText` undefined (main), AFTER = the patched `msteamsChannelOutbound.sanitizeText` export.
```
[BEFORE main]  OUT: "Here is your summary.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `grep -E 'PV-123' /tmp/out.txt (agent)` failed\nThe report is ready."
[AFTER patch]  OUT: "Here is your summary.\nThe report is ready."
```
BEFORE: the `⚠️ 🛠️ … (agent) failed` banner survives into outbound text. AFTER: the banner line is removed, both prose lines preserved.

### Why main leaks

`src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts` applies `handler.sanitizeText` only when present (`:795`). On main `msteamsChannelOutbound` has no `sanitizeText`, so the shared gate is skipped and text passes through verbatim. This PR adds `sanitizeText: ({ text }) => sanitizeAssistantVisibleText(text)` at `extensions/msteams/src/channel.ts:444`, mirroring the merged Google Chat fix #95084. Canonical sanitizer: `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.ts` → `stripAssistantInternalTraceLines()`.

**Proof limitation** (consistent with the PR's existing note): the AFTER side exercises the hook through a faithful re-implementation of the `deliver.ts` gate (the real gate is module-internal, not exported), not a live MS Teams socket send.

target.title: fix(secrets): collect persona-level TTS provider SecretRefs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Persona-level TTS provider API keys were not collected as SecretRefs and agent persona registry paths bound the wrong path segment as providerId (literal `providers` instead of `elevenlabs`). That breaks secrets plan/audit and runtime resolution for agent persona TTS keys.

Fixes #89607

## Summary

The secret collector walks `messages.tts.providers.*.apiKey` but does not walk `messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` or `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`. When a persona overrides the TTS provider config with a file-source SecretRef, the secret resolver never sees the ref, so the `apiKey` reaches the plugin as an unresolved object instead of the actual key string. The plugin then reports `not configured`.

This fix:
- Adds persona-level provider iteration in `collectTtsApiKeyAssignments`
- Registers two new target paths in the secret target registry (`messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` and `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`)
- Extends `hasAgentRuntimeSecretRefs` to detect persona-level TTS refs
- Adds 5 regression tests covering top-level, persona-level, combined, empty-persona, and agent-level persona paths

Closes #89607

## Evidence

Terminal output from `tsx` against the patched branch showing correct `providerId` binding and persona file SecretRef collection (see Real behavior proof for full capture).

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Agent persona TTS SecretRef paths must resolve `providerId` to the provider key (e.g. `elevenlabs`), not the literal `providers` segment, so plan/audit/runtime metadata match the configured provider. Persona-level file SecretRefs must be collected under `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS arm64, Node v22, OpenClaw branch `fix/tts-persona-secretref` at `/tmp/oc-89636`, commit after providerId index fix.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  ```bash
  cd /tmp/oc-89636
  pnpm exec vitest run src/secrets/target-registry.test.ts src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.test.ts
  pnpm exec tsx /tmp/proof-tts-providerid.mjs
  pnpm exec tsx /tmp/proof-tts-collect.mjs
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from the patched source:

  ```console
  ✓ src/secrets/target-registry.test.ts (10 tests)
  ✓ src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.test.ts (5 tests)
  Test Files  2 passed (2)
  Tests  15 passed (15)

  $ pnpm exec tsx /tmp/proof-tts-providerid.mjs
  {"path":"agents.list.0.tts.personas.narrator.providers.elevenlabs.apiKey","entryId":"agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey","providerId":"elevenlabs"}
  {"path":"agents.list.0.tts.providers.elevenlabs.apiKey","entryId":"agents.list[].tts.providers.*.apiKey","providerId":"elevenlabs"}
  {"path":"messages.tts.personas.narrator.providers.elevenlabs.apiKey","entryId":"messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey","providerId":"elevenlabs"}
  {"path":"messages.tts.providers.elevenlabs.apiKey","entryId":"messages.tts.providers.*.apiKey","providerId":"elevenlabs"}

  $ pnpm exec tsx /tmp/proof-tts-collect.mjs
  assignments:
  {"path":"agents.list.0.tts.personas.narrator.providers.elevenlabs.apiKey","ref":{"source":"file","provider":"default","id":"/tmp/redacted-narrator-key.txt"}}
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Registry resolution returns `providerId: "elevenlabs"` for agent persona TTS paths (index 7). Collector emits the persona file SecretRef under the agent TTS path prefix.
- **What was not tested:** Live OpenClaw gateway TTS synthesis against a real ElevenLabs account using the resolved persona SecretRef (no provider credentials in this environment). Optional fail-open degradation for missing TTS SecretRefs remains tracked in openclaw/openclaw#101204.


## Rank-up follow-up (2026-07-09)

ClawSweeper P1: include global persona TTS refs in agent-runtime targets.

- Added `messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` to `STATIC_AGENT_RUNTIME_BASE_TARGET_IDS`
- Extended the agent-runtime target coverage assertion to require both global and agent-level persona paths

Terminal confirmation on branch head:

```console
$ node ./node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/cli/command-secret-targets.test.ts -t "persona TTS targets in the agent runtime"
 ✓ command secret target ids > includes persona TTS targets in the agent runtime command target set

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 39 skipped (40)
```

Still not tested: live `openclaw infer tts convert` with a file-source persona SecretRef (no TTS provider credentials in this environment).

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.0. #3995
  • In addition to the existing input format, the config-file input for the codeql-action/init step will soon support a new [owner/]repo[@ref][:path] format. All components except the repository name are optional. If omitted, owner defaults to the same owner as the repository the analysis is running for, ref to main, and path to .github/codeql-action.yaml. target.title: [codex] Add doctor lint for agent model runtime policy drift
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw doctor --lint` did not report a useful warning when active agent model refs drifted away from explicit per-model `agentRuntime` policies. This is one diagnostic slice of #84212: it helps surface contradictory config, but it does not hard-fail config save or reload.

## Why This Change Was Made

The issue's full config-save/reload rejection path is product-sensitive because existing schema-valid configs may become hard failures. This PR keeps the change warning-only and scoped to doctor lint:

- active agent model refs warn when an agent has explicit runtime policies but no matching policy for the active ref
- stale per-model runtime policy keys warn when no active model ref uses them
- policy matching mirrors runtime resolution for bare model IDs, provider-qualified IDs, normalized provider aliases, and provider wildcards
- per-agent checks account for inherited default runtime policies

## User Impact

Users get a direct `doctor --lint` warning for model/runtime-policy drift instead of discovering it later as model routing or no-candidate runtime degradation. This is partial mitigation only; #84212 should remain open for the broader config persistence/reload decision unless maintainers decide warning-only lint coverage is sufficient.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed:

Doctor lint should warn when the active model has no matching explicit runtime policy, while accepting a bare model key that runtime resolution treats as matching a provider-qualified active model.

Real environment tested:

WSL Ubuntu, source checkout at `12b3f07565d`, built source launcher `node openclaw.mjs`, and isolated local config/state directories. No provider or network call was needed.

Exact steps to reproduce or validate:

1. Create an isolated config with active model `openai/gpt-5.5` and only an `openai/gpt-5.4` runtime policy.
2. Run `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-99619-proof/state OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/openclaw-99619-proof/openclaw.json node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --json --only core/doctor/agent-model-runtime-policies`.
3. Create a second isolated config with active model `openai/gpt-5.5` and bare runtime-policy key `gpt-5.5`.
4. Run `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-99619-proof/state-bare OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/openclaw-99619-proof/openclaw-bare-key.json node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --json --only core/doctor/agent-model-runtime-policies`.

Evidence after fix:

The drift fixture returned structured JSON with `"ok": false`, `"checksRun": 1`, and exactly two warnings:

- `agents.defaults.model selects openai/gpt-5.5, but agents.defaults has explicit agentRuntime policies with no matching model key.`
- `agents.defaults.models.openai/gpt-5.4.agentRuntime.id sets a runtime for openai/gpt-5.4, but no active model ref in agents.defaults uses that model key.`

The bare-key fixture returned:

```json
{"ok":true,"checksRun":1,"checksSkipped":43,"findings":[]}
```

Observed result:

The real built launcher emitted both expected drift warnings and no bare-key false positive. The shell status was `0` for both launcher invocations, so this proof asserts the structured JSON and findings, not an exit-code change.

What was not tested:

No config save/reload hard failure, provider call, or gateway session was tested. Exit-code propagation through the generic built launcher is not part of this patch.

## Supporting verification

At `12b3f07565d` in WSL:

- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/commands/doctor-lint.test.ts src/flows/doctor-core-checks.ts` -> passed
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json src/commands/doctor-lint.test.ts src/flows/doctor-core-checks.ts` -> 0 warnings, 0 errors
- `OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor-lint.test.ts src/flows/doctor-core-checks.test.ts src/flows/doctor-lint-flow.test.ts src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts --reporter=dot` -> passed, 103 tests across two routed shards
- `git diff --check` -> passed

target.title: fix(gateway): require shared secret for tailscale serve auth
target.body:
## Summary
Fixes #57110.

Adds an opt-in `gateway.auth.requireTailscaleSharedSecret` setting for Tailscale Serve Control UI/WebSocket access. When enabled, a remote Control UI WebSocket request must pass verified Tailscale identity and the configured token or password before it is accepted, and toggling the setting at runtime invalidates Tailscale-authenticated sessions established under the previous policy.

## Root cause
`src/gateway/auth.ts:598` kept the existing tokenless Tailscale Serve path separate from shared-secret auth:

```before
if (canUseTailscaleHeaderAuth && !hasExplicitSharedSecretAuth(connectAuth)) {
  const tailscaleCheck = await resolveVerifiedTailscaleUser({
    req,
    tailscaleWhois,
  });
  if (tailscaleCheck.ok) {
    limiter?.reset(ip, rateLimitScope);
    return {
      ok: true,
      method: "tailscale",
      user: tailscaleCheck.user.login,
    };
  }
}
```

There was no accepted config field that required both verified Tailscale Serve identity and the configured Gateway shared secret.

## Fix
`src/gateway/auth.ts:574` now handles the opt-in layered path before the tokenless Tailscale branch:

```after
if (canUseTailscaleHeaderAuth && auth.requireTailscaleSharedSecret === true) {
  const tailscaleCheck = await resolveVerifiedTailscaleUser({
    req,
    tailscaleWhois,
  });
  if (!tailscaleCheck.ok) {
    return tailscaleCheck;
  }
  const sharedSecretResult = authorizeSharedSecretAuth({
    auth,
    connectAuth,
    limiter,
    ip,
    rateLimitScope,
  });
  if (!sharedSecretResult.ok) {
    return sharedSecretResult;
  }
  return {
    ...sharedSecretResult,
    user: tailscaleCheck.user.login,
  };
}
```

The new config key is wired through config types, strict schema validation, sparse auth override merging, schema help/labels, and Gateway docs.

## Session invalidation when the flag changes
Enabling `requireTailscaleSharedSecret` at runtime is a security tightening, so live sessions that were validated under the looser policy must be dropped. Two changes make that happen through the existing shared-gateway session-generation machinery instead of a new mechanism:

- `src/gateway/server/ws-shared-generation.ts` folds `requireTailscaleSharedSecret` into the session generation digest, but only when the flag is enabled. Default deployments keep their existing generation, so already issued shared-auth device tokens survive an upgrade, while flipping the flag rotates the generation and forces re-authentication.
- `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.ts` tags a tokenless Tailscale Control UI session with that generation so it participates in generation-based invalidation. Without this, a session accepted while the flag was off stayed connected after the operator enabled it. The narrow `usesSharedGatewayAuth` used for shared-auth device-token issuance is unchanged, so Tailscale sessions do not start issuing shared-auth device tokens.

The reload and RPC config-write paths already disconnect stale shared-auth clients through `resolveSharedGatewaySessionGenerationForConfig`, so both cover the flag toggle with no new call sites.

## Why this is the right boundary
Gateway auth already owns Tailscale Serve identity verification and shared token/password checks. Keeping the composition in `authorizeGatewayConnectCore` preserves the existing HTTP behavior, keeps the tokenless Control UI WebSocket behavior as the default, and lets existing shared-auth generation handling see layered successful sessions as `token` or `password` sessions for rotation and issued device-token tracking.

HTTP API endpoints remain unchanged because Tailscale header auth is still limited to the `ws-control-ui` auth surface.

## Verification
- `PATH=/opt/node/bin:$PATH node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/auth.test.ts src/gateway/startup-auth.test.ts src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts src/config/schema.test.ts` passed 3 shards: 23 tooling checks, 464 Gateway checks, and 56 runtime-config checks.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over `websocket`/`unix` transport would hang forever on `initialize`/RPC when a peer accepted TCP but never completed the WebSocket upgrade. Pending frames never flush and the client never sees a transport exit, so the run cannot fail closed or reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` that sets `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
- Both TCP and Unix upgrade paths consume that builder.
- Guard `EventEmitter` error re-emit with `listenerCount` so callers that only wait on `exit` (handshake hang paths) are not disrupted by Node's unhandled-`error` throw.
- Regressions observe production wiring in source (knip-safe) and prove stalled-handshake exit + `initialize` failure with a short test-only hang floor.

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Codex app-server endpoint that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin `initialize`/RPC forever on that attempt.

**After:** Handshake waits fail closed after 30s (`Opening handshake has timed out` → transport `exit` / client error), so the run can stop or recover instead of hanging.

## Evidence

Head: `a02be68e1107857c4808cc9e93e1af5b10c7f1f1`

Executable negative control + fix proof:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text
stdout | extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts > Codex app-server websocket transport > negative control: ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING on never-upgrade peer
[codex handshake negative control] outcome=still-pending readyState=0 wait_ms=300 without_handshakeTimeout=true
 ✓ |extension-codex| extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts > Codex app-server websocket transport > negative control: ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING on never-upgrade peer 306ms
[codex handshake proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=200 code=1006 handshakeTimeout_ms=200 production_ms=30000
    187|       `[codex handshake negative control] outcome=${outcome} readyStat…
The latest test that might've caused the error is "negative control: ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING on never-upgrade peer". It might mean one of the following:

```

- **Negative control (executable):** plain `ws.WebSocket` with **no** `handshakeTimeout` against the same TCP-accept / never-upgrade fixture stays `CONNECTING` / `still-pending` after 300ms.
- **After fix:** `createWebSocketTransport` with `handshakeTimeoutMs: 200` emits `exit` (~200ms); production wiring asserts `CODEX_APP_SERVER_WS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` in the private builder.

target.title: fix(reef): bound inbox websocket open waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Reef inbox monitoring uses the WHATWG `WebSocket` (not the `ws` package), so there is no `handshakeTimeout` option. `ReefInboxConnection.live()` only settles on `close` / `error` / channel `abort`. When a peer accepts TCP but never completes the websocket upgrade, `start()` waits forever on `await live()` and the reconnect backoff loop never advances.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `REEF_INBOX_WEBSOCKET_OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` open-wait floor inside `live()`.
- On timeout: reject with `reef inbox websocket open timed out` (before `close`) so `start()` takes the existing catch/backoff path.
- Clear the timer on successful `open` so healthy long-lived inbox sockets are unaffected.
- Optional constructor `openTimeoutMs` defaults to 30s for production; tests use a short stand-in.

No new config/env surface. Does not switch Reef onto the `ws` package.

Note: open [#106456](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/106456) bounds relay HTTP JSON reads in the same `transport.ts`; this PR only touches the inbox websocket open wait and should rebase cleanly.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Reef relay that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin the inbox reconnect loop forever until the channel aborted.

**After:** Open waits fail closed after 30s and the existing reconnect backoff continues.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`
- Production caller: `extensions/reef/src/channel.ts` → `ReefInboxConnection.start`
- Sibling intent: Slack/Mattermost/Signal 30s handshake floors (Reef cannot use `ws` `handshakeTimeout`)
- Regression: `extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts`

### Caller-path Vitest

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text

[reef open-wait proof] timeout_then_reconnect=true socket_attempts=2 openTimeout_ms=40
 ✓ returns control to reconnect when the websocket never opens 309ms
[reef open-wait live proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=506 openTimeout_ms=200

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

## Real behavior proof

**Commands run:**
```bash

```

**Before fix:**
`live()` had no open-wait timer; a never-opening socket left `start()` blocked until channel abort.

**After fix:**
Production default open-wait is 30s. Against a hang factory / TCP peer that never upgrades, `live()` rejects and `start()` reconnects.

**Evidence after fix:**
```text
[reef open-wait proof] timeout_then_reconnect=true socket_attempts=2 openTimeout_ms=40
[reef open-wait live proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=506 openTimeout_ms=200
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

**What was not tested:**
Live Reef relay credentials; full 30s production floor (tests use 40ms / 200ms stand-ins with source wiring asserting `30_000`); REST `fetch` hang floors on `ReefTransportClient.request` (separate surface; see also #106456).

target.title: fix(skills): globally-installed ClawHub skills falsely show as not tracked [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

Closes #105530

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who install a ClawHub skill **globally** (`openclaw skills install <slug> --global`, living under the managed dir `~/.openclaw/skills/<slug>` and tracked in the **global** lockfile `~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`) would see the skill falsely reported as `ClawHub link invalid` in `openclaw skills status` and the Control UI, with the message:

> Skill `<slug>` has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.

The skill is in fact correctly installed and tracked - just in the global lockfile, not the workspace one.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` read the ClawHub lockfile exclusively from the workspace directory (`readClawHubSkillsLockfileStatusSync(workspaceDir)`) and passed that single read to `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` for every non-bundled skill. For a globally-installed skill (`source: "openclaw-managed"`), the tracking entry lives in the **managed** lockfile at `<dirname(managedSkillsDir)>/.clawhub/lock.json`, so the workspace lookup misses it and returns `invalid`.

The fix resolves the link status for `openclaw-managed` skills against the managed lockfile (and the managed parent dir, so the expected-install-dir check matches the skill dir) instead of the workspace lockfile. Workspace-local skills are unchanged. Detection uses the loader-assigned `source` rather than a lexical path check, because managed skill roots may contain symlinks whose resolved `baseDir` sits outside the `managedSkillsDir` tree.

## User Impact

Globally installed ClawHub skills now show as correctly `linked` in `openclaw skills status` and the Control UI skills view, instead of a false `ClawHub link invalid` / "not tracked" warning. Workspace-local skill status is unaffected.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof captured on Windows 10 by running the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` against real on-disk lockfiles (standalone `tsx` repro script run locally; before/after output below). The script creates a managed (global) install - skill dir under `managedSkillsDir` with `.clawhub/origin.json`, plus a global lockfile at `<managedParent>/.clawhub/lock.json` tracking it - and a separate workspace whose own lockfile does **not** track the skill.

BEFORE (unpatched main) - the globally-installed skill is falsely `invalid`, read against the **workspace** lockfile:

```
"skillSource": "openclaw-managed",
"clawhub": {
  "status": "invalid",
  "valid": false,
  "reason": "Skill \"agentreceipt\" has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.",
  "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-workspace-fYctHw\\.clawhub\\lock.json"
}
```

AFTER (this patch) - the same skill is correctly `linked`, read against the **managed (global)** lockfile:

```
"skillSource": "openclaw-managed",
"clawhub": {
  "status": "linked",
  "valid": true,
  "registry": "https://clawhub.ai",
  "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "installedVersion": "1.2.3",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-managed-83CHpB\\.clawhub\\lock.json"
}
```

Regression tests added in `src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts`:
- links a globally-installed skill via the managed lockfile (asserts `status: "linked"`)
- reports a globally-installed skill as `invalid` when it is absent from the managed lockfile (guards against falsely linking)

Full skill-status suite passes (`pnpm test -- src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts` -> 13 passed, 1 skipped on win32).

## Real Behavior Proof

- Behavior addressed: Globally installed ClawHub skills (`source: "openclaw-managed"`) are falsely reported as `invalid` / "not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile" because `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` only consults the workspace lockfile.
- Real environment tested: Windows 10, Node v22.22.3, OpenClaw main @ 50e5ffcd25, running the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` function from `src/skills/discovery/status.ts` via `pnpm exec tsx`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: a standalone `tsx` script builds a managed/global install (skill dir + `.clawhub/origin.json` + global lockfile tracking the slug) and a separate workspace whose lockfile omits the slug, then calls `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus(workspaceDir, { managedSkillsDir, entries })` and prints the resolved `clawhub` status.
- Evidence after fix:
```
AFTER (patched):
"clawhub": { "status": "linked", "valid": true, "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-managed-83CHpB\\.clawhub\\lock.json" }

BEFORE (unpatched main):
"clawhub": { "status": "invalid", "valid": false,
  "reason": "Skill \"agentreceipt\" has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-workspace-fYctHw\\.clawhub\\lock.json" }
```
- Observed result after fix: The globally-installed skill resolves to `status: "linked"` against the managed (global) lockfile instead of `invalid` against the workspace lockfile. The `lockPath` in the resolved status now points at the global lockfile.
- What was not tested: End-to-end through a running gateway / live Control UI render; the real `openclaw skills status` CLI against a real `~/.openclaw` home. The proof exercises the real production status function with real on-disk lockfiles, which is the exact code path the CLI and UI consume.

## Human Verification

Verified: the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` code path with real on-disk managed + workspace lockfiles (before/after), scoped `pnpm test` for the skills status suite, `pnpm tsgo` (type check), `pnpm format:check`, scoped `oxlint --type-aware` on the changed files. Not verified: Swift (skipped on Windows), full `pnpm test` suite, live Control UI rendering. Note: local `pnpm build` (tsdown) hit a V8 out-of-memory crash on this Windows machine (a known low-memory local-env quirk, unrelated to this 3-line logic change); relying on CI's build check on a properly-sized runner.

## Security Impact

- Does this change authentication, authorization, or trust boundaries? No.
- Does this change credential, secret, or token handling? No.
- Does this change sandboxing or process isolation? No.
- Does this change network boundaries or external API calls? No.
- Does this introduce a new trust boundary or change an existing one? No.

No CODEOWNERS secops paths are touched (`src/skills/` is not secops-owned). The change only affects which local lockfile is consulted for a status display.

## Compatibility / Migration

No config, API, CLI, or lockfile-format changes. The set of inputs/outputs of `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` is unchanged; only the accuracy of the `clawhub` status for globally-installed skills improves. No migration required.

## Failure Recovery

If the managed lockfile read regresses, globally-installed skills would revert to the prior `invalid` / "not tracked" display behavior - a cosmetic status misreport, not a crash or data loss. The change is read-only with respect to lockfiles (no writes), so there is no risk of lockfile corruption. Reverting the commit fully restores prior behavior.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: A skill whose loader-assigned `source` is `openclaw-managed` but whose lockfile entry legitimately lives in the workspace lockfile would now be looked up in the managed lockfile. **Mitigation**: managed skills are, by definition, installed under `managedSkillsDir` and tracked in the managed lockfile; workspace-local skills use other `source` values and are unaffected. Added a regression test for the "absent from managed lockfile" case to ensure such a skill still reports `invalid` rather than falsely `linked`.
- **Risk**: Competing/sibling PR on the same issue. **Mitigation**: this PR supplies the real-behavior-proof (real production-function output with real on-disk lockfiles, before/after) that the issue's proof gate requires, rather than a screenshot.

## Review Conversations

- [x] I will respond to review comments in the review conversation where they were left.
- [x] I understand review conversations belong to the reviewer and I should not resolve them myself unless requested.

target.title: fix(android): localize chat bubble role labels
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Android chat bubbles still had two visible role labels that bypassed the native localization path: the pending tools bubble (`Tools`) and the streaming assistant bubble (`OpenClaw · Live`). That made the chat UI inconsistent with the rest of the localized Android role labels.

## Why This Change Was Made

This updates the chat bubble role-label helper so all chat role labels, including tools and live assistant states, resolve through literal `nativeString(...)` calls. Keeping the literals in the helper preserves native i18n extraction while avoiding per-bubble hard-coded English labels.

target.title: fix(qqbot): bound gateway websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QQBot gateway websocket creation set headers/proxy agent but not `handshakeTimeout`. `gateway-connection` sets `isConnecting=true` until `open` or `close`; when a peer accepts TCP but never completes the websocket upgrade, that flag stays true forever and reconnect is skipped (`Already connecting, skip`). Slack relay, Mattermost, and Signal already bound handshake waits at 30s.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Bake `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` into `createQQWSClient` via `QQBOT_WEBSOCKET_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- Timeout-induced `close` already clears `isConnecting` and drives `scheduleReconnect` — no gateway-connection logic change.
- Regressions assert constructor wiring and prove a real TCP hang fails at ~30s.

No new config/env surface.

Note: open [#99075](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/99075) bounds `maxPayload` in the same factory; this PR only adds handshake timeout and should rebase cleanly after that lands.

## User Impact

**Before:** A QQBot gateway peer that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin the channel in a permanent connecting state with no reconnect.

**After:** Handshake waits fail closed after 30s (`Opening handshake has timed out` / close 1006), clearing `isConnecting` so reconnect continues.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/ws-client.ts`
- Production caller: `gateway-connection.ts` → `createQQWSClient`
- Sibling: Slack relay / Mattermost / Signal `handshakeTimeout: 30_000`
- Regression: `ws-client.test.ts`, `ws-client.ws-handshake.test.ts`

target.title: fix(sessions): cap in-memory session history to prevent unbounded growth
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Long-running autonomous sessions accumulate message turns indefinitely in `SessionHistorySseState.sentHistory.messages` without any pruning. The in-memory array grows without bound, leading to OOM crashes on constrained hosts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two improvements:

**1. Early raw-message trimming (new):** The constructor now trims the initial raw messages to `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES × 2` (1000) BEFORE the full `projectChatDisplayMessages` pass when inline mode is active. This avoids projecting and transforming thousands of raw messages only to discard most of them immediately.

**2. Projected-message capping:** `appendInlineMessage` caps `sentHistory.messages` at `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES` (500) after every append via `trimHistoryMessages`. Combined with early raw trimming, this ensures both the raw-input and projected-output paths are bounded.

When trimming, `hasMore` is set to `true` and `nextCursor` points to the first retained seq so callers can signal older-history availability. The cap only applies to inline (unpaginated) mode.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes during long-running autonomous sessions
- Older history remains available via `refreshAsync()` or paginated snapshots
- Normal interactive sessions (≤500 turns) are completely unaffected
- Inline SSE appends continue to work for recent history

## Persistent Data Model — No migration needed

The change does not modify any serialized data format, SQLite schema, config surface, or storage layout. The `sentHistory` array is strictly in-memory state reconstructed from transcript reads on each session load.

## Evidence

**Head SHA:** `9516b52031a209d4c3cb379725669d9f13a810bc`

### Rank-up P1 — authenticated Gateway real calls (SSE + cursor)

Exact-head patch exercised through production Gateway HTTP:

- Auth: shared-secret bearer (`Authorization: Bearer test-gateway-token-…`) + `operator.read` WS connect
- Path: `GET /sessions/{sessionKey}/history` Accept `text/event-stream` → `SessionHistorySseState`
- Cursor pages: same endpoint with `?limit=&cursor=`

```text

[gateway-history-proof] gateway authenticated ws+http port=39000 head=PR#105339-patched
[gateway-history-proof] INIT SSE history: count=500 hasMore=true nextCursor=21
[gateway-history-proof] APPEND: +20 transcript updates emitted (live SSE message/history events)
[gateway-history-proof] REFRESH/REOPEN SSE: count=500 hasMore=true last=append-19 nextCursor=41
[gateway-history-proof] PAGE1 limit=100: count=100 hasMore=true nextCursor=441

[gateway-history-proof] PROOF PASS — authenticated Gateway SSE bound + cursor pages
```

Note: ClawSweeper still needs an explicit maintainer decision on the **500-message unpaginated compatibility boundary**; this proof addresses the Gateway artifact Rank-up only.

A/B vitest + constructor/append unit coverage from earlier Evidence remains supplementary.

target.title: Fix/OpenAI device code request timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running OpenAI Codex device-code login (`openclaw models auth login --provider openai --device-code`, or the equivalent configure/wizard auth choice) could hang forever when a single `auth.openai.com` HTTP request stopped responding.

Before this patch, the flow enforced a 15-minute poll-loop deadline around authorization waiting, and callers could cancel via `AbortSignal`, but the three HTTP calls for user-code request, authorization poll, and token exchange had no per-request operation deadline covering both headers and body reads. A stalled TCP/proxy/blackhole response, or a server that returned headers and then stalled the body, could leave the CLI spinner stuck.

## Why This Change Was Made

Treat each device-code HTTP call as one timed operation: headers fetch plus bounded body read under `buildOAuthRequestSignal` (caller `AbortSignal` composed with `AbortSignal.timeout`, 30s, aligned with the sibling ChatGPT browser OAuth token request timeout). Poll requests clamp that timeout to the remaining 15-minute authorization deadline and retry only on operation timeout (including post-header body stalls) until the overall deadline expires. Caller cancel (Ctrl-C / wizard abort) remains distinguishable and does not retry. User-code and token-exchange timeouts fail fast with a clear error.

Body/fetch aborts rethrow the composed signal reason so undici `AbortError` collapse does not erase `TimeoutError` vs caller cancel distinguishability.

Scope stays OpenAI Codex device-code login HTTP only; browser OAuth and other providers are unchanged.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung device-code HTTP request (or a post-header body stall) could block `models auth login --device-code` indefinitely, even past the advertised 15-minute authorization window, while still depending on the overall poll deadline for happy-path waiting.

**After:** Each device-code request+body read aborts after 30 seconds (or sooner near the overall deadline). Poll timeouts retry within the 15-minute window; caller cancel aborts immediately without retry; user-code and token-exchange stalls surface an explicit timeout error instead of hanging forever.

## Evidence

- `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.ts` — `buildOAuthRequestSignal` composes caller cancel + 30s operation deadline across fetch + body read; poll retries only on operation timeout
- Regression: `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts`
  - hung user-code / token-exchange abort with timeout error
  - poll retries after `TimeoutError` and completes
  - caller cancel during hung fetch / poll wait / post-header body stall does not retry or map to timeout
  - real `node:http` partial-body stall coverage
  - success path asserts fetches carry an `AbortSignal`

### Unit regression

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** OpenAI Codex device-code login no longer leaves individual HTTP operations unbounded when the remote endpoint stops responding before headers return, or returns headers and then stalls the body; caller cancel remains distinct from operation timeout.
- **Canonical reachability path:** Operator runs device-code auth → `loginOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `requestOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `pollOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `exchangeOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `runOpenAICodexDeviceCodeRequest` → `buildOAuthRequestSignal` (`AbortSignal.any([caller, AbortSignal.timeout(...)])`) + `readOpenAICodexDeviceBody`.

Preserves current-main caller `AbortSignal` cancellation from provider sign-in. Does not migrate this path onto `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in this change.

target.title: refactor(process): route bounded commands through Execa
target.body:
Related: #105920
Follow-up to #105939

AI-assisted. I understand the execution, cancellation, output, and platform behavior changed here.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where bounded one-shot commands across core and bundled plugins still bypassed OpenClaw's canonical Execa-backed execution layer, leaving inconsistent timeout, environment, output-cap, error, and process-tree behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

This routes suitable bounded command sites through the canonical process wrapper, adds a buffered SDK seam for plugin-owned callers, and splits the execution implementation into focused spawn, output, result, termination, and runner modules behind the existing `src/process/exec.ts` facade. OpenClaw-specific contracts remain owned by the wrapper: argv-only Windows batch safety, console-codepage decoding, capped capture, abort/timeout semantics, inherited-pipe draining, and process-tree termination. Specialized interactive, streaming, supervised, daemon, tunnel, watcher, IPC, and detached-restart processes remain direct spawns by design.

The Windows termination path now waits for bounded `taskkill` ownership to settle before aborting Execa, avoiding a live-root PID reuse race.

Docker and SSH sandbox commands use one explicit 100 MiB output cap, so their full-buffer contract neither inherits Execa's hidden default nor permits unbounded gateway heap growth.

QA Lab node probing passes restricted environments as the exact base environment, preserving the old `execFile({ env })` isolation contract.

## User Impact

No intended user-visible behavior change. Operators and plugin developers get more consistent bounded-command behavior, while long-lived and interactive process owners keep their specialized lifecycle paths.

target.title: fix(usage): ignore invalid Z.ai reset timestamps
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Z.ai usage fetch converts `nextResetTime` with `new Date(...).getTime()`. Invalid strings produce `NaN`, which is then stored on the usage window as `resetAt` and can poison downstream reset/cooldown logic that expects a finite timestamp or an unset value.

This is provider-contract hardening at the Z.ai usage parser boundary: untrusted quota metadata must not introduce non-finite numbers into domain objects.

## Why This Change Was Made

In `src/infra/provider-usage.fetch.zai.ts`, keep `resetAt` only when `Number.isFinite(parsedReset)` so invalid reset strings are ignored while valid ISO timestamps still populate `resetAt`.

## User Impact

**Before:** Invalid `nextResetTime` values could yield `resetAt: NaN` on Z.ai usage windows.
**After:** Invalid reset strings leave `resetAt` undefined; valid ISO resets still work.

## Evidence

Branch: `codex/zai-invalid-reset-time` | Base: `upstream/main` | Head: `ed45a4bf` | Node: v24.18.0 — Windows

### Diff summary

```text
src/infra/provider-usage.fetch.zai.ts       | finite reset guard on parsed nextResetTime
src/infra/provider-usage.fetch.zai.test.ts  | invalid + valid ISO reset regression
```

What was not tested: a live upstream quota payload that actually contains an invalid `nextResetTime` string (this account returns a coding-plan error with empty windows).

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** Invalid truthy `nextResetTime` no longer becomes `resetAt: NaN` on Z.ai usage windows; valid ISO resets still populate finite `resetAt`. The same production `fetchZaiUsage` path is used for live authenticated calls and parser hardening checks.
**Environment tested:** Windows, Node v24.18.0, patched branch `ed45a4bf`; production `fetchZaiUsage` imported from `src/infra/provider-usage.fetch.zai.ts` via `node --import tsx` (script: `zai-invalid-reset-proof.mts`).
**Steps run after the patch:**

1. Run `node --import tsx --no-warnings zai-invalid-reset-proof.mts` against production `fetchZaiUsage`.
2. With `ZAI_API_KEY` set (not logged), call the live `https://api.z.ai/api/monitor/usage/quota/limit` endpoint through the same production function.
3. On the same production function, feed a synthetic 200 JSON body containing `nextResetTime: "not-a-date"` plus a valid ISO monthly reset and inspect parsed windows.

**Evidence after fix:**

```text
$ node --import tsx --no-warnings zai-invalid-reset-proof.mts

live fetchZaiUsage:
{

}
parser control: nextResetTime="not-a-date" -> getTime=NaN Number.isNaN=true
production fetchZaiUsage invalid+valid payload: {
```

target.title: fix(agents): reject with AbortError when tool execution is cancelled
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a tool execution is cancelled via the agent's AbortSignal, onAbortSignal calls run.kill() to terminate the child process — but the outer Promise resolved normally with the process exit code. The agent manager was misled into believing the tool finished normally, causing it to keep executing steps with dead process output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The process exit handler always called resolve(buildExecForegroundResult(...)) regardless of whether the exit was caused by an abort signal. Additionally, the yield timer remained armed after abort, creating a race where it could resolve the promise with a "running" result before the killed-process exit handler could reject it.

## User Impact

- Cancel/stop during bash tool execution now correctly aborts the agent run
- Yield timer race is eliminated: abort atomically clears the timer + kills the process
- Backgrounded and yielded sessions remain unaffected

## Evidence

**Head SHA:** `afe3cc92cdbbfff2573062dc6441a98f8b02e4d9`

### Rank-up P1 — agent stop during exec (before/after)

# Agent-path abort-during-exec proof — PR #105726

Fixes #105681. No secrets. Local `sleep` only.

## Production chain

`run AbortController` (sessions.abort / embedded handle.abort)
→ `wrapToolWithAbortSignal`
→ `toToolDefinitions.execute`
→ `createExecTool.onAbortSignal`

## BEFORE (unpatched main-shaped exec)

```text
[2026-07-13T17:12:41.631Z] PROOF START — agent-path stop during exec (#105726)
[2026-07-13T17:12:41.637Z] cwd=/Users/sm/zw_openclaw pid=10277
[2026-07-13T17:12:41.639Z] tools wired: exec, proof_step2_marker
[2026-07-13T17:12:41.639Z] TURN START: step1=exec(sleep), planned step2=proof_step2_marker
[2026-07-13T17:12:42.142Z] OPERATOR STOP: runAbort.abort() (agent run cancel / sessions.abort shape)
[2026-07-13T17:12:42.153Z] STEP1 RESOLVED (unexpected): {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Command aborted by signal SIGTERM"}],"details":{"status":"failed","exitCode":null,"exitSignal":"SIGTERM","failureKind":"signal","exitReason":"manual-cancel",...
[2026-07-13T17:12:42.153Z] TURN CONTINUES (bug path): invoking step2
[2026-07-13T17:12:42.241Z] step2Calls=0
[2026-07-13T17:12:42.241Z] PROOF FAIL
```

Unpatched exec **resolves** a normal tool result (`SIGTERM` / failed details) after kill, so the agent-manager loop can continue to later steps.

## AFTER (PR #105726 patch)

```text
[2026-07-13T17:14:21.826Z] PROOF START — agent-path stop during exec (#105726)
[2026-07-13T17:14:21.829Z] patch: toolAborted + AbortError reject + yieldTimer clear (PR #105726)
[2026-07-13T17:14:21.832Z] tools wired: exec, proof_step2_marker
[2026-07-13T17:14:21.832Z] TURN START: step1=exec(sleep 30), planned step2=proof_step2_marker
[2026-07-13T17:14:22.334Z] OPERATOR STOP: runAbort.abort() (sessions.abort / embedded handle.abort shape)
[2026-07-13T17:14:22.341Z] STEP1 REJECTED: name=AbortError message=Tool execution was aborted
[2026-07-13T17:14:22.341Z] TURN END: step1 aborted — agent manager skips later tool steps
[2026-07-13T17:14:22.341Z] step2Calls=0
[2026-07-13T17:14:22.342Z] PROOF PASS — abort ends turn; no later tool step
```

Patched exec **rejects** `AbortError`; turn ends; `proof_step2_marker` never executes (`step2Calls=0`).

target.title: fix(zalo): make poll error backoff abort-aware
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Zalo polling error backoff used a bare `setTimeout(5000)` that ignored `abortSignal` / stop. After a non-timeout poll error, Gateway stop or account switch could leave the backoff sleep running for the full 5s (orphan timer / delayed poll continuation). Sibling Signal `sse-reconnect` and Slack reconnect already use `sleepWithAbort`.

Open [#104017](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104017) adds Bot API request timeouts; it does not fix poll error backoff sleep.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the bare sleep with abort-aware backoff matching Signal/Slack:

```ts
try {
  await sleepWithAbort(5000, abortSignal);
} catch {
  return;
}
```

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** After a poll transport error, abort/stop still waited out (or left running) a 5s `setTimeout` before the polling loop fully wound down.

**After:** Abort during error backoff ends the sleep immediately and returns from the poll loop.

## Evidence

- Production caller: `startPollingLoop` inside `monitorZaloProvider` (polling mode)

target.title: fix(discord): add timeout to guarded gateway metadata fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Discord gateway metadata HTTP through `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded` could hang in DNS/proxy preflight because the `/gateway/bot` deadline lived only in `init.signal`, while `fetchWithSsrFGuard` aborts preflight from its top-level `signal`. A stalled Discord API / proxy preflight could block gateway startup until process restart.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper P1: forward the existing `withAbortTimeout` AbortSignal as the guard's top-level `signal`, and keep a single deadline owner:

- When `init.signal` is present (production `/gateway/bot` path): pass `{ signal: callerSignal }` only — no second `timeoutMs` timer
- When unsignaled: install `timeoutMs` hang floor (default 30s / `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs`)
- Thread resolved `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs` through `createDiscordGatewayMetadataFetch` / invalid-proxy fallback for the unsignaled hang floor

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Discord metadata DNS/proxy preflight ignored the gateway metadata abort signal and could hang forever.
